issues.legal_issue: A person allotted land in excess of lawful entitlement has no enforceable right to require the authority to sell the excess land merely by offering payment.
material_facts: Five displaced persons received agricultural land in excess of their lawful entitlement because of an inadvertent error in calculating their allotments.
The excess allotment was cancelled, and the allottees then applied to purchase the excess land by payment or adjustment against compensation.
The authority rejected the application, but the High Court held that the allottees were entitled to require the sale.
issues.conclusion: The governing rule conferred discretion on the Settlement Commissioner and did not obligate the authority to sell the excess land; the High Court’s contrary ruling was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 73(2)(ii) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, uses “may” and confers discretion rather than creating an enforceable right to purchase excess land. A Constitution Bench in Mohinder Singh v. Chief Settlement Commissioner, interpreting the pari materia provision in Rule 62, held that “may” cannot be read as “shall.” Construing the rule to compel sale could reward mistaken or otherwise excessive allotments at the expense of rightful claimants and defeat the Rules’ compensatory purpose.

predicates.appeal_from_order_requiring_sale_of_exce: An appellate court is reviewing an order that required an authority to sell excess allotted land to the recipients of that allotment.
predicates.excess_allotment_exceeded_lawful_entitle: The recipients were allotted more land than they were lawfully entitled to receive.
predicates.governing_rule_uses_discretionary_transf: The governing rule gives the authority discretion over transferring excess land rather than making transfer mandatory.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an order compelling sale of land allotted beyond the recipients’ entitlement under a rule that makes transfer discretionary, the authority may refuse the sale.

issues.legal_issue: A new legal plea that was not raised in the proceedings below may be declined when it is advanced for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The allottees relied on a statute-based plea that had not been included in their writ petitions or urged before the High Court.
They raised that plea for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal after having enjoyed the benefit of the excess allotment for many years.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the allottees to raise the new plea for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a plea based on the Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Act, 1976, because it had not been raised in the writ petition or before the High Court and was advanced for the first time in the Supreme Court; the Court also noted the allottees’ long enjoyment of an undeserved benefit. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

rule.if: appeal_before_supreme_court and new_legal_plea_not_raised_in_lower_courts and plea_raised_for_first_time_on_appeal and party_long_enjoyed_undue_benefit

predicates.appeal_before_supreme_court: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.new_legal_plea_not_raised_in_lower_court: The party did not raise the legal plea in the proceedings before the lower courts.
predicates.plea_raised_for_first_time_on_appeal: The party advances the legal plea for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal.
predicates.party_long_enjoyed_undue_benefit: The party had enjoyed an undue benefit for a substantial period before raising the plea.

issues.definition: If a party raises a legal plea for the first time in a Supreme Court appeal after omitting it below and having long enjoyed an undue benefit, the Court may decline to entertain that plea.
